concepts.name: Classic Four-Stage DTM: Stage Characteristics and Transitions
key_dimensions: Specific birth rate (BR) and death rate (DR) values and trends in each stage
Net population growth curve shape across all four stages — identifying peak growth stage (Stage 2)
Common UPSC trap: confusing Stage 3 (falling BR) with Stage 2 (falling DR only)
Real-world country examples for each stage and how they shift over time

concepts.name: Stage 1 — High Stationary Stage: Pre-Industrial Demographics
key_dimensions: Drivers of high birth rates: agrarian economy, son preference, lack of contraception, child labour utility
Drivers of high death rates: famines, epidemics, poor sanitation, absence of modern medicine
Near-zero net population growth despite high vital rates — the 'demographic equilibrium trap'
Contemporary societies still partially in Stage 1 (e.g., parts of Sub-Saharan Africa) and policy implications

concepts.name: Stage 2 — Early Expanding Stage: Mortality Decline and Population Explosion
key_dimensions: Factors causing DR to fall faster than BR: public health, vaccines, green revolution, improved nutrition
This stage produces the maximum population growth rate — the demographic dividend's precondition
India's experience in Stage 2 (1950s–1980s) and its consequences for current age structure
UPSC trap: why BR remains high even as DR falls — cultural lag, son preference, economic incentives

concepts.name: Stage 3 — Late Expanding Stage: Fertility Transition and Slowing Growth
key_dimensions: Drivers of falling BR: urbanisation, female education, contraception access, rising opportunity cost of children
Population still growing but at a decelerating rate — absolute numbers vs. growth rate distinction
India's current positioning in Stage 3: TFR at 2.0 (NFHS-5) but momentum effect sustaining growth
Intra-country variation: Kerala/Tamil Nadu at Stage 4 threshold vs. Bihar/UP still in Stage 2–3 transition

concepts.name: Stage 4 — Low Stationary Stage: Near-Zero Growth and Ageing Societies
key_dimensions: Both BR and DR low and roughly equal — replacement-level fertility (TFR ~2.1)
Emerging challenges: ageing population, shrinking workforce, pension burden, healthcare costs
Country examples: Japan, Germany, Italy — policy responses (pro-natalist incentives, immigration)
UPSC trap: Stage 4 is NOT zero population — immigration and momentum can still cause growth

concepts.name: Stage 5 — Sub-Replacement Fertility: Post-Transition Decline (Extended DTM)
key_dimensions: TFR falling below 2.1 leading to natural population decline without immigration
Countries: South Korea (TFR ~0.78), Japan, Eastern European nations
Policy panic: natalist policies, immigration liberalisation, robotic workforce discussions
UPSC relevance: why Stage 5 was not in original DTM — historical limitation of the model

concepts.name: Total Fertility Rate (TFR) as the Core Metric of DTM
key_dimensions: Definition: average number of children per woman over reproductive lifetime — distinguished from crude birth rate
Replacement-level TFR of 2.1 — why it's not exactly 2 (accounting for infant mortality and sex ratio at birth)
India's TFR trajectory: 6.0 (1950) → 3.4 (2000) → 2.0 (NFHS-5, 2019–21) — policy significance
UPSC trap: TFR below replacement does NOT immediately mean population decline due to demographic momentum

concepts.name: Demographic Momentum: Population Growth After Replacement Fertility is Achieved
key_dimensions: Mechanism: large cohort of young people entering reproductive age sustains births even at low TFR
India's population projected to peak ~1.65 billion around 2064 despite TFR at replacement level
Policy implication: why family planning success today won't stop growth for decades
UPSC trap: conflating demographic momentum with population explosion — they represent opposite phases

concepts.name: Demographic Dividend: Window of Opportunity in DTM Stage 3
key_dimensions: Definition: economic growth potential from a temporarily high working-age population ratio
Preconditions to harvest dividend: education, healthcare, employment generation, gender inclusion
India's dividend window: estimated 2020–2040 — comparison with East Asian Tiger economies
UPSC trap: demographic dividend is NOT automatic — it requires enabling policy environment; can become a 'demographic disaster'

concepts.name: Epidemiological Transition Model (Omran) and Its Link to DTM
key_dimensions: Omran's model explains the DR decline in Stage 2 through shifting disease burden: pestilence → degenerative diseases
Four stages: Age of Pestilence and Famine → Receding Pandemics → Degenerative Diseases → Delayed Degenerative Diseases
India's 'polarised' epidemiological transition: double burden of communicable and non-communicable diseases simultaneously
UPSC relevance: links DTM to health policy, NCD burden, and Universal Health Coverage debates

concepts.name: Critiques and Limitations of the Classic DTM
key_dimensions: Eurocentrism: model derived from Western European experience — may not universally apply
Assumes a single linear pathway — ignores countries where fertility declined without industrialisation (e.g., Bangladesh, Sri Lanka)
Does not account for migration as a demographic variable — a major gap for contemporary analysis
UPSC angle: what modified/alternative models exist — Second Demographic Transition (SDT), multiphasic response theory

concepts.name: Second Demographic Transition (SDT) Theory
key_dimensions: Proposed by Van de Kaa and Lesthaeghe — explains sub-replacement fertility in post-industrial societies
Drivers: individualism, cohabitation, delayed marriage, childfree lifestyles, gender equality beyond economic factors
Distinguishes from first transition: first driven by child mortality decline; second driven by value change
UPSC trap: SDT is distinct from DTM Stage 5 — SDT emphasises socio-cultural shifts, not just economic factors

concepts.name: Age-Sex Pyramid Shapes Corresponding to DTM Stages
key_dimensions: Stage 1–2: broad base, narrow apex (expansive pyramid) — high youth dependency
Stage 3: transitional pyramid — narrowing base, bulging middle
Stage 4–5: constrictive/urn-shaped pyramid — narrow base, broad middle, growing apex
UPSC application: reading pyramids to identify country's DTM stage and predict future demographic challenges

concepts.name: Dependency Ratio and Its Variation Across DTM Stages
key_dimensions: Definition: ratio of dependent population (0–14 and 65+) to working-age population (15–64)
Stage 2: high youth dependency; Stage 4–5: high old-age dependency; Stage 3: low total dependency = dividend window
India's current dependency ratio ~47 (favourable) vs. Japan ~70 (ageing burden)
UPSC trap: low dependency ratio doesn't equal prosperity — quality of employment and skill-matching matter

concepts.name: Role of Female Education and Women's Empowerment in Driving DTM Stage 3
key_dimensions: Empirical link: each additional year of female schooling reduces TFR by ~0.3–0.5 children
Mechanisms: delayed marriage age, contraceptive use, economic opportunity cost of childbearing
Kerala Model — high literacy, low TFR despite moderate income — challenges purely economic DTM explanations
UPSC angle: connects DTM to gender policy, SDG-5, PCPNDT Act, and population stabilisation strategy

concepts.name: Urbanisation as an Accelerator of Fertility Decline in DTM
key_dimensions: Urban areas show lower TFR universally: smaller living spaces, higher child-rearing costs, career aspirations
India: Urban TFR ~1.6 vs. Rural TFR ~2.1 (NFHS-5) — urban areas already below replacement
Circular causality: DTM Stage 3 drives urbanisation AND urbanisation deepens Stage 3 transition
UPSC trap: urbanisation alone doesn't explain DTM — rural Bangladesh achieved low TFR without rapid urbanisation

concepts.name: India's National Population Policy (NPP 2000) and Its Alignment with DTM Stage 3
key_dimensions: Target-free approach replacing coercive sterilisation — shift from demographic targets to reproductive rights
NPP 2000 goal: achieve replacement-level TFR by 2010 (delayed — achieved ~2020)
District-level variation: 146 high-focus districts (EAG states) still in Stage 2–3, needing targeted interventions
UPSC trap: NPP 2000 does NOT prescribe a two-child norm as a legal mandate — it is a voluntary goal

concepts.name: Migration's Role as the 'Missing Variable' in DTM
key_dimensions: Original DTM only considers natural increase (BR–DR) — ignores migration-driven demographic change
In Stage 4–5 countries, immigration offsets population decline (e.g., Germany, Canada, Australia)
Brain drain from Stage 2–3 countries distorts domestic demographic dividend calculations
UPSC relevance: refugee crises, NRC, migration policy debates — where DTM provides analytical backdrop

concepts.name: Demographic Transition in the Context of Sustainable Development and Resource Pressure
key_dimensions: Stage 2 population explosion → pressure on food, water, land, energy — Malthusian concerns revisited
Stage 4–5 ageing → different resource pressures: healthcare, pension, eldercare infrastructure
'Demographic bonus vs. burden' framing in climate change adaptation and SDG planning
UPSC angle: connects DTM to carrying capacity, ecological footprint, and India's climate commitments

concepts.name: Comparative DTM Positioning: India vs. China vs. Sub-Saharan Africa vs. Europe
key_dimensions: China: accelerated Stage 3→4 due to One Child Policy — now facing Stage 5 crisis with shrinking workforce
Sub-Saharan Africa: largely in Stage 2 — highest population growth globally, projected 4 billion by 2100
India vs. China: India's later transition means younger age structure — strategic advantage vs. China's ageing
UPSC trap: not all developing countries follow same DTM trajectory — fertility decline possible without full industrialisation
